claims.text: Local atomic-scale strain induced by compositional inhomogeneities governs premature surface melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Local atomic-scale strain lowers the energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
A uniformly mixed nanoparticle can serve as a minimal-strain initial state and baseline.
Controlled compositional inhomogeneities generate localized lattice strain, particularly at the nanoparticle surface.
The relevant structural mediators are localized surface lattice strain and altered surface atomic coordination.
Strained regions initiate premelting at the nanoparticle surface by reducing the barrier to atomic rearrangement.
Early atomic diffusion originating at strained surface regions propagates into the nanoparticle core as temperature increases.
Nanoparticles with intentionally introduced local strain will have a lower surface-premelting onset temperature than uniform, strain-minimized nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with intentionally introduced local strain will exhibit greater atomic mobility than the baseline under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism should hold for high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles approximately 5–20 nm in diameter under high-temperature conditions.
The quantitative effects of element-specific interactions on local strain and melting behavior are uncertain.
The scaling of the proposed strain effect with nanoparticle size is uncertain.

Failure of engineered surface strain to produce a statistically significant reduction in premelting temperature, or observation of similar melting behavior in strained and baseline particles, would falsify the hypothesis.
